Genesis.author: Jews and Christians have long received Genesis as the first of the five books of Moses, and many still hold that view [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]] [[bo:18623]]. The book itself does not name its author [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.date: If Moses wrote it, in the wilderness after the Exodus: about 1445 BC on the early dating [[bo:18623]], or by 1240 BC at the latest on the later one [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.to: The people of Israel, to help them understand their roots in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob [[bo:18623]], and as the groundwork for the rest of the books of Moses [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.why: The book of beginnings. God, the good King of all, makes the world and gives people the task of caring for it under him [[bible:Genesis 1:26-28]]. When they turn from him, he promises that a child of the woman will one day crush the serpent [[bible:Genesis 3:15]] [[ks:1]].
Genesis.story: Everything that follows grows from here. God promises Abraham a family, a land and blessing for every nation on earth [[bible:Genesis 12:1-3]], and the rest of the Bible tells how he keeps those promises [[ks:1]]. Genesis ends with the family small and far from home in Egypt, yet kept alive by God’s grace, not by their own goodness [[ks:1]] [[bible:Genesis 50:20]]. Scholars picture the whole Bible as a symphony in four movements, creation, fall, redemption and re-creation: Genesis plays the first two and begins the third, and the Bible’s last chapters return to its garden, river and tree of life [[dl:Genesis]] [[bible:Revelation 22:1-2]].
Genesis.genre: Narrative history, organised under ten headings, “these are the generations of…” (Hebrew toledot, best translated “history”) [[eob:Genesis]] [[bo:18623]].
Genesis.debate: How Genesis was written: many modern scholars see it as woven from older sources (J, E, D and P) given final shape after the exile, a theory others reject [[eob:Genesis]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; and how its creation and flood accounts compare with other ancient Near Eastern stories, such as the Gilgamesh and Atrahasis epics [[nabre:genesis/6]] [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.structureNote: The book falls into two halves, the early history (1–11) and the story of the patriarchs (12–50) [[eob:Genesis]]; the outline below follows the main characters of the text.

Exodus.author: Very early Jewish tradition held that Moses wrote it, and many still hold that view [[eob:Book-Exodus]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; the book records Moses writing down God’s words [[bible:Exodus 24:4]]. It does not name its author [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.date: The events: about 1446 BC on the early dating, or about 1260 BC on the late dating, which links the city of Raamses (1:11) with Pharaoh Rameses II; both are held by evangelical scholars [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]. The evidence is not enough for a final decision, but points to the second half of the second millennium BC [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.to: The people of Israel, as the story of how God made them his own nation [[nabre:exodus/0]].
Exodus.why: God rescues his people. He hears Israel’s cry in Egypt, breaks Pharaoh’s power, makes a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, and comes to live among them in the tabernacle [[ks:2]] [[nabre:exodus/0]]. The rescue, the law and the tabernacle all say one thing: God is with his people as their Saviour and King, and the exodus is the greatest act of salvation in the Old Testament [[dl:Exodus]].
Exodus.story: The family promised to Abraham has become a great nation [[bible:Exodus 1:7]]. The book ends with God’s glory filling the tent at the centre of the camp [[bible:Exodus 40:34]] [[ks:2]]. The rescue from slavery becomes the Bible’s great picture of salvation, and the New Testament calls Jesus our Passover lamb [[bible:1 Corinthians 5:7]].
Exodus.genre: About half narrative, the first nineteen chapters, and about half law and instructions for worship [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.debate: The date of the Exodus [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]; why no Egyptian king is named and why Egyptian monuments are silent, which is expected since defeats were not recorded [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; how its laws compare with Hammurabi’s code, with which direct parallels are fairly few [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; and whether, as many modern scholars think, it was woven from older sources [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Exodus.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into eight parts [[nabre:exodus/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Leviticus.author: It presents its laws as given by God through Moses [[bible:Leviticus 26:46]], and many scholars defend that view [[eob:Leviticus]]. The book does not name its author [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.date: On the traditional view, the time at Sinai, soon after the Exodus [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.to: The people of Israel and their priests. Its laws are meant to shape the whole way of life of those who hear them [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.why: How can a holy God live among his people? Leviticus answers: he himself provides the way, through sacrifice that covers sin, through cleansing, and through a holy life lived before him [[ks:3]] [[eob:Leviticus]]. Behind every law stands one truth: God is holy, so only those made clean can come near him [[dl:Leviticus]] [[bible:Leviticus 11:45]].
Leviticus.story: It stands at the centre of the five books of Moses [[nabre:leviticus/0]]. Its sacrifices and its priests point forward to Jesus, the great high priest whose one sacrifice brings full forgiveness [[ks:3]] [[bible:Hebrews 9:11-14]]. Its call still stands: be holy, because God is holy [[bible:1 Peter 1:15-16]].
Leviticus.genre: Laws for worship and daily life, with a few short narratives [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.debate: How and when the book was composed: many critical scholars see it as Priestly material finished around 550 BC or later [[eob:Leviticus]] [[nabre:leviticus/0]]; what the verb kipper, “atone”, means: to wipe away, to cover, or to pay a ransom [[eob:Leviticus]]; and whether the Holiness laws came before or after Ezekiel, which cannot be shown with certainty [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.structureNote: The outline follows the five parts of the NABRE introduction [[nabre:leviticus/0]].

Numbers.author: Like the other books of the Pentateuch, it has traditionally been credited to Moses [[easton:Numbers-Book]]; it says Moses wrote down the list of Israel’s journeys [[bible:Numbers 33:2]].
Numbers.date: The events cover about thirty-eight years, from the second year after the Exodus to the fortieth [[easton:Numbers-Book]] [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.to: The people of Israel, who were about to enter the land God had promised [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.why: Israel marches through the wilderness with God at the centre of the camp. A generation that would not trust him dies on the way, yet God does not take back his promise, and a new generation stands ready to enter the land [[ks:4]] [[nabre:numbers/0]]. Even when his people grumble and rebel, God keeps his covenant, guides them and provides for them [[dl:Numbers]].
Numbers.story: Even the hired prophet Balaam is made to bless Israel, and he sees a star and a king rising from Jacob [[bible:Numbers 24:17]], which Christians read as pointing to Christ [[ks:4]]. Hebrews looks back on the wilderness as a warning not to harden our hearts [[bible:Hebrews 3:7-19]].
Numbers.genre: Law and history together, with two censuses, travel lists and the poetic oracles of Balaam [[nabre:numbers/0]].
structure: Rebellion and forty years in the wilderness
A new generation prepares to enter the land
Numbers.debate: How the book was composed, since many modern scholars see the Pentateuch as woven from several sources [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; the route through the wilderness, since the list of stages is not complete and many places are not known [[nabre:numbers/33]]; and what exactly Moses’s sin at Meribah was, which the text does not make clear [[nabre:numbers/20]].
Numbers.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:numbers/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Deuteronomy.author: It is presented as three speeches of Moses [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]], and says Moses wrote this law down [[bible:Deuteronomy 31:9]]. Those who hold that he wrote it point to its likeness to Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]; an editor added the account of his death [[bo:885]].
Deuteronomy.date: If by Moses, the 1300s or 1200s BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]], or about 1406 BC on the early dating of the Exodus [[bo:885]].
Deuteronomy.to: The new generation of Israel on the plains of Moab, about to enter the promised land [[nabre:deuteronomy/1]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 4:13]].
Deuteronomy.why: Moses’ last words before Israel enters the land. Love the LORD your God with all your heart [[bible:Deuteronomy 6:5]]: obedience here is a grateful answer to his love, not a way of earning it [[ks:5]].
Deuteronomy.story: Moses looks ahead to Israel’s failure and exile, and beyond it to a day when God will change their hearts himself [[bible:Deuteronomy 30:6]] [[ks:5]]. He also promises a prophet like him [[bible:Deuteronomy 18:15]], fulfilled in Jesus [[bible:Acts 3:22-26]]. Jesus answered every temptation with words from this book [[bible:Matthew 4:4]]. It is one of the Old Testament books the New Testament quotes most, and Moses’ promise of a prophet like him kept Israel watching until John the Baptist and Jesus came [[dl:Deuteronomy]] [[bible:John 1:21]].
Deuteronomy.genre: Speeches of Moses that follow the pattern of an ancient covenant treaty, with laws, blessings and curses [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 1:1]].
structure: Third address: covenant renewal and farewell
Deuteronomy.debate: Whether Moses wrote it, or, as many critical scholars hold, it was written in King Josiah’s time or composed over several centuries [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]] [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; its relation to the book of the law found in the temple in 622 BC [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; and how closely it follows Hittite treaty forms [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]. Its Greek name, “second law”, can mislead, since it is not a simple repeat of the law [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three addresses of Moses and the account of his death [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Joshua.author: The book does not say. The Talmud names Joshua, perhaps because he “wrote these words” of the covenant renewal [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[bible:Joshua 24:26]].
Joshua.date: There are no clear markers [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]]. A conservative view dates the writing between 1375 and 1045 BC [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]].
Joshua.to: Israel, to show how the LORD gave them the land and how they might prosper in it [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], and to warn them against losing it [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.why: God keeps his word: Israel enters the land promised to Abraham. The victories are the LORD’s, not Israel’s, and the people are called to choose to serve him [[ks:6]] [[bible:Joshua 24:15]].
Joshua.story: A second part of the promise to Abraham comes true [[bible:Joshua 21:43-45]] [[ks:6]]. Joshua’s name means “the LORD saves”, the same name as Jesus [[nabre:numbers/13]]. Hebrews says the rest Joshua gave was a picture of a deeper rest still to come [[bible:Hebrews 4:8-9]]. “Jesus” is simply the Greek form of the name Joshua, and the New Testament sees in Jesus the leader who brings God’s people into their lasting inheritance [[dl:Joshua]].
Joshua.genre: History, the first of the books the Hebrew Bible calls the Former Prophets [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], with lists of tribal lands that preserve older traditions [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.debate: When and by whom it was written: critical scholars suggest the 600s BC or the exile, as part of a larger history from Deuteronomy to Kings [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[nabre:joshua/0]]; how its swift conquest fits Judges 1, which suggests a slower settlement [[nabre:joshua/0]]; and how to read the destruction it describes alongside the New Testament command to love enemies [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:joshua/0]]; the outline below follows them, with the conquest in two halves.

Judges.author: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition named Samuel; many scholars think a writer of the early monarchy compiled it from older records [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.date: The final editing reflects the early days of Israel’s kings [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]. The period itself began about 1370–1360 BC on the early dating of the Exodus, or near the end of the 1200s BC on the later one [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.to: Israel under its first kings, explaining why the tribes did not take all the land and pointing toward a king who would shepherd the people [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.why: Israel lives in the promised land, yet keeps forgetting God. Again and again they turn to idols, cry out, and are rescued by a judge God sends [[bible:Judges 2:16-19]], showing his patience with a stubborn people [[ks:7]].
Judges.story: The book ends in chaos: there was no king, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes [[bible:Judges 21:25]]. It leaves us longing for a good king, a longing met in David and finally in Jesus [[ks:7]]. For all their flaws, Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are remembered for their faith [[bible:Hebrews 11:32-34]], and their story shows how much God’s people need a champion to fight for them [[dl:Judges]].
Judges.genre: Hero stories of twelve judges from different regions, framed by an introduction and two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]] [[tosn:Judges 17:1-21:25]].
structure: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes
Judges.debate: How long the period of the judges lasted, which depends on the date of the Exodus [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]; and whether the book argues for David’s rule rather than Saul’s, as some scholars think [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.structureNote: The outline follows the book’s introduction, the stories of the judges and its two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].

Ruth.author: Unknown [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]]. Since it closes with David’s family line, it was probably written after David began to reign, perhaps by someone close to him such as Samuel, Nathan or Abiathar [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.date: The events took place around 1100 BC, in the days of the judges [[tosn:Ruth 1:1]]. It was likely written after David became king [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.to: Israel, perhaps to show that David’s family was the chosen royal line, and to explain how a faithful Moabite woman became part of Israel [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.why: A quiet story of loyal love in a dark time. A foreign widow trusts Israel’s God, and through the kindness of Boaz, God works unseen to bring hope out of loss [[ks:8]] [[bible:Ruth 2:12]]. God is seldom mentioned by the narrator, yet his hidden care shapes every turn of the story [[dl:Ruth]].
Ruth.story: Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David [[bible:Ruth 4:17]], the answer to Judges’ cry for a king [[ks:8]]. She is named in Jesus’ family tree [[bible:Matthew 1:5]], a sign that God’s blessing was always meant for all nations [[ks:8]].
Ruth.genre: A short story that ends with a family line of ten generations, from Perez to David [[tosn:Ruth 4:18-22]].
Ruth.debate: When it was written, which affects what its purpose was [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].

1 Samuel.author: Unknown. It cannot have been Samuel alone, since his death is reported in 25:1 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Some suggest Samuel with the prophets Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29), but the real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.date: Its final form comes some time after Solomon’s death and the division of the kingdom in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.to: Israel, about what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.why: God gives Israel a king. Hannah sings that God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud [[bible:1 Samuel 2:7-8]], and that is the story of Saul, who turns from God, and young David, a man after God’s own heart [[ks:9]] [[bible:1 Samuel 13:14]].
1 Samuel.story: God looks at the heart, not the outside [[bible:1 Samuel 16:7]]. Hannah’s song already looks ahead to God’s anointed king [[bible:1 Samuel 2:10]], and the line of kings that begins here leads to Jesus [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]] [[ks:9]]. The young shepherd who risked his life for his sheep [[bible:1 Samuel 17:34-35]] points ahead to the good shepherd who lays down his life for his [[dl:Samuel]] [[bible:John 10:11]].
1 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as Hannah’s song (2:1–10) [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book until the Greek translators split them in two [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it, and how its mixed feelings about kingship fit together; the book resolves them in chapter 12 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

2 Samuel.author: Unknown. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book, and its real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.date: David ruled the strongest kingdom of the region about 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]]. The book reached its final form some time after the kingdom split in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.to: Israel, about David’s reign and what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.why: David reigns, and God makes him a promise: his family will rule forever [[bible:2 Samuel 7:12-16]]. David’s great failure with Bathsheba shows that even the best king is not the final answer [[ks:9]].
2 Samuel.story: The promise to David becomes the heart of Israel’s hope for a Messiah [[ks:9]], fulfilled in the eternal reign of Jesus Christ [[tosn:2 Samuel 7:19]] [[bible:Luke 1:32-33]].
2 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as David’s laments and his song in chapter 22 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Chapters 21–24 are arranged by topic, not by time [[tosn:2 Samuel 21:1–24:25]].
2 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it and when it took its final form [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

1 Kings.author: Unknown; the book is anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition in the Talmud names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. It draws on official royal annals, “the chronicles of the kings” [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.date: The events run from Solomon’s accession to the divided kingdoms [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]; Solomon’s fourth year was about 967 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 6:1]] and the kingdom split under Rehoboam in 931 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 12:1]]. 1 and 2 Kings were completed in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.to: The exiles, who were asking how and why Jerusalem and the temple could fall [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.why: Solomon’s reign shines like a return to paradise, with wisdom, peace and the temple filled with God’s glory [[bible:1 Kings 8:10-11]]. Then his heart turns to other gods, and the kingdom splits in two [[ks:10]].
1 Kings.story: Through it all God’s word proves true: what his prophets say comes to pass [[ks:10]] [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Elijah’s stand on Mount Carmel shows that the LORD alone is God [[bible:1 Kings 18:39]]. Jesus is the greater king, wiser than Solomon [[bible:Matthew 12:42]]. Through all the turmoil, a son of David stays on the throne in Jerusalem for about three and a half centuries, which is why the Gospels take such care to show that Jesus is the Son of David [[dl:Kings]].
1 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, not a modern history textbook [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.debate: Who compiled it, and how the dates given for the kings of Israel and Judah fit together into one timeline [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

2 Kings.author: Unknown; 1 and 2 Kings are anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.date: It covers the divided kingdoms, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]], Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC, and Jehoiachin’s release about 561 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Written in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.to: The exiles, asking how and why the temple and David’s throne had fallen [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.why: Both kingdoms walk away from God, and both go into exile, Israel to Assyria and Judah to Babylon [[bible:2 Kings 17:7]] [[bible:2 Kings 25:21]]. God’s warnings were patient, and his word came true [[ks:10]]. The book is written for people in exile, to explain why it happened and to show that God had not given up on David’s line [[dl:Kings]].
2 Kings.story: The book ends with a quiet hope: David’s heir is released from prison in Babylon [[bible:2 Kings 25:27-30]]. God had promised David a lamp that would not go out [[bible:2 Kings 8:19]], and he had not forgotten [[ks:10]].
2 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, drawing on royal annals [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.debate: How the reigns of the kings fit into one timeline, and how the book compares with Assyrian and Babylonian records [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]] [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

1 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler” [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]]. The Talmud says Ezra wrote it, and many scholars agree, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.to: Jews living in Jerusalem under Persian rule after the exile [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.why: Israel’s story retold for the people back from exile, to give them hope. From Adam to David, it shows that God’s promise to David still stands and that worship of God belongs at the centre of life [[ks:11]] [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.story: It is fundamentally a book of hope: though there was no king on the throne, God’s kingdom would still come [[ks:11]]. God’s promise to David here [[bible:1 Chronicles 17:11-14]] looks ahead to the Son of David who reigns forever [[bible:Luke 1:32-33]].
1 Chronicles.genre: Genealogies (chapters 1–9) and the reign of David (chapters 10–29) [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether the same author wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

2 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler”; the Talmud names Ezra, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.to: Jews in Jerusalem under Persian rule, for whom temple worship mattered greatly [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.why: Solomon builds the temple, and the kings of Judah rise or fall by whether they seek the LORD. Whenever a king humbles himself and prays, God hears [[bible:2 Chronicles 7:14]] [[ks:11]].
2 Chronicles.story: It ends not with ruin but with an invitation: King Cyrus lets God’s people go up to Jerusalem [[bible:2 Chronicles 36:23]]. In the Hebrew Bible it is the last book, so the Old Testament ends looking forward [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]] [[ks:11]].
2 Chronicles.genre: History drawing on earlier records, retelling Samuel and Kings with its own concerns [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether its author also wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

Ezra.author: Many believe Ezra himself collected and wrote the material; parts are told in his own words [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.date: The events run from Cyrus’s decree after he took Babylon in 539 BC to Ezra’s work under Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]]. Ezra came about 13 years before Nehemiah, who arrived in 445 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.to: The Jews who returned from exile under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.why: God keeps his promise to bring his people home. He moves a Persian king to let them return [[tosn:Ezra 1:1]], the temple is rebuilt, and Ezra sets his heart to study, live and teach God’s law [[bible:Ezra 7:10]] [[ks:12]]. In Ezra and Nehemiah the whole community, not just its leaders, rebuilds and turns back to the LORD together [[dl:Ezra-Nehemiah]].
Ezra.story: Home again, but not yet free: the people are still under foreign kings and still struggle with sin [[bible:Ezra 9:9]] [[ks:12]]. The return shows God is faithful, while making clear that a deeper rescue is still needed [[ks:12]].
Ezra.genre: History with official letters written in Aramaic and a first-person account by Ezra [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
structure: The first return and the temple
Ezra.debate: Whether Ezra came before Nehemiah [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]], and how to understand the divorces of chapter 10, for which the law gave no clear instructions [[tosn:Ezra 10:4]].

Nehemiah.author: Nehemiah tells much of it in his own words [[bible:Nehemiah 1:1]]. Ezra and Nehemiah formed one book in the early Hebrew Bible [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.date: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in 445 BC, under Artaxerxes I [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.to: The Jews who had returned to Judah under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.why: A man of prayer leads God’s people to rebuild Jerusalem’s walls in fifty-two days [[bible:Nehemiah 6:15-16]], and the people gather to hear God’s word and renew their promise to him [[bible:Nehemiah 8:8]] [[ks:12]].
Nehemiah.story: It closes the Old Testament history with the people back in the land but still weak and still failing [[ks:12]] [[bible:Nehemiah 13:10-11]]. The longing for a new heart and a true king carries over into the prophets and the Gospels [[ks:12]]. Its honest last chapter, with the old sins creeping back, leaves a question hanging: will God’s people only repeat the past [[dl:Ezra-Nehemiah]]? Only a new heart can answer it [[bible:Jeremiah 31:33]].
Nehemiah.genre: First-person memoir with lists and a covenant ceremony [[bible:Nehemiah 7:5]] [[bible:Nehemiah 9:38]].
Nehemiah.debate: The exact order of Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s work; the book’s message is clear either way [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].

Esther.author: Unknown. Esther 9:20 says Mordecai “wrote these things”, which may mean he wrote part or all of it [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.date: Set under Xerxes, who died in 465 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]]. When it was written is uncertain: some say shortly after 465 BC, others much later [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.to: Jews living in the Persian empire, and to explain the feast of Purim [[bible:Esther 9:26-28]].
Esther.why: God is never named, yet he is everywhere in this story. Through a brave queen and a string of surprising reversals, he saves his people from a plot to wipe them out [[ks:13]] [[bible:Esther 4:14]].
Esther.story: No plan to destroy God’s people can succeed, because God keeps his covenant [[ks:13]]. The feast of Purim celebrates how sorrow was turned into joy [[bible:Esther 9:22]], and the story shows God’s hand guiding ordinary events [[tosn:Esther 7:9]]. For Christian readers, more was at stake than one nation’s survival: through this people the promised Messiah would come, and God was steering history toward him [[dl:Esther]].
Esther.genre: A court story written by someone who knew Persian court life well [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.debate: When and why it was written, and the extra passages in the Greek version [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]] [[tbd:005:Esther, Additions to]].

Psalms.author: Many writers. The Hebrew titles credit David with 73 psalms, Asaph with 12 and the sons of Korah with 11, Solomon with two, and Moses and Ethan with one each [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]]. The titles were added early and are a reasonably reliable guide [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.date: From David’s time, around 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]], to after the exile [[tosn:Psalm 126:1–6]]. The collection was complete before the Greek translation at the end of the 200s BC [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.to: God’s people at worship, in every situation of life [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.why: The prayer book and songbook of God’s people, with every human feeling brought before God [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]]. Its great message is that the LORD reigns [[bible:Psalm 93:1]], so the whole book moves toward praise [[ks:15]]. Joy is its strongest note, and it is quoted in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament book [[dl:Psalms]] [[gbp:4]].
Psalms.story: The five books of Psalms move from David’s reign, through the grief of exile, to the hope of a new David [[ks:15]]. Jesus and the apostles often use the Psalms to show who he is [[tosn:Psalm 1:1–6]], and the book ends with everything that has breath praising the LORD [[bible:Psalm 150:6]].
Psalms.genre: Poetry in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, each of the first four ending with a doxology [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.debate: What the titles mean: “of David” usually means by David, but with groups it may mean from their collection [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].

Job.author: Unknown; no one is named as author [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.date: Uncertain. Most modern scholars think it was written after the exile, around the 400s BC; others place it near the end of the exile, in Solomon’s time, or in the age of the patriarchs [[tbd:002:Book of Job]]. Job’s wealth in livestock fits the patriarchal era [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.to: Anyone asking why good people suffer [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].
Job.why: A good man loses everything and cries out to God. Job’s friends insist he must have sinned, but the book shows they are wrong [[bible:Job 42:7]]. God answers Job not with an explanation but with himself, the Creator who rules all things [[ks:14]] [[bible:Job 38:1-4]]. Underneath runs a deeper question: who is truly wise? Only God is, and the right response to him is trust [[dl:Job]] [[bible:Job 42:5-6]].
Job.story: Real wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord [[bible:Job 28:28]] [[ks:14]]. Job learns to trust God where he cannot see. The Bible’s final answer to suffering comes in Jesus, who defeated evil by suffering himself [[ks:14]].
Job.genre: A prose prologue and epilogue around long poetic speeches [[tbd:002:Book of Job]] [[bsn:Job 4:1–31:40]].
Job.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether it combines earlier writings [[tbd:002:Book of Job]].

Proverbs.author: Several writers, named in the book’s seven or more sections: Solomon (970–930 BC) for the main parts, “the wise”, Agur and King Lemuel [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]]. Whether 1:1 means Solomon wrote chapters 1–9 is best left open [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
Proverbs.date: Solomon’s reign, 970–930 BC, with more of his proverbs gathered by King Hezekiah’s men (728–686 BC) [[tosn:Proverbs 25:1–29:27]] [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
Proverbs.to: Young people especially, “to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the young man” [[bible:Proverbs 1:4]].
Proverbs.why: Wisdom for everyday life, with all of life lived under God. It begins and builds on one foundation: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge [[bible:Proverbs 1:7]] [[ks:16]].
Proverbs.story: Where Psalms teaches us to praise God, Proverbs teaches us to fear and honour him in the ordinary details of work, speech, money and family [[ks:16]]. Christians see Jesus as the fullest expression of God’s wisdom, one greater than Solomon [[ks:16]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 1:30]]. Its sayings are not promises for every case but true observations about how God’s world usually works, which Job and Ecclesiastes balance [[dl:Proverbs]].
Proverbs.genre: Poems and two-line sayings, often in contrasting pairs [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]]. They describe how life generally works under God, not guarantees [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].
structure: A father’s lessons and Lady Wisdom
Agur and Lemuel; the worthy woman
Proverbs.debate: Its close parallel with the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope in 22:17–23:11, and which came first [[tbd:016:Proverbs, Book of]].

Ecclesiastes.author: The Teacher, Qoheleth, “son of David, king in Jerusalem” [[bible:Ecclesiastes 1:1]], traditionally Solomon [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]].
Ecclesiastes.date: If Solomon, around 940 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]]. Fragments from the 100s BC were found at Qumran [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]].
Ecclesiastes.why: An honest look at life under the sun: pleasure, work and wisdom cannot satisfy on their own [[bible:Ecclesiastes 2:11]]. So enjoy God’s gifts with thanks, and fear God and keep his commandments [[bible:Ecclesiastes 12:13]] [[ks:17]].
Ecclesiastes.story: It speaks to a world that, since the fall, often feels frustrating [[ks:17]]. Paul says creation was subjected to futility in hope [[bible:Romans 8:20-21]], and in Christ a new creation has begun [[bible:2 Corinthians 5:17]] [[ks:17]]. When Paul says creation was subjected to futility, his Greek word is the one the ancient Greek translation used for Ecclesiastes’ motto, “meaningless” [[dl:Ecclesiastes]] [[bible:Romans 8:20]].
Ecclesiastes.genre: Reflections and sayings, with a closing note by an editor [[tosn:Ecclesiastes 12:9–14]].
structure: Youth, age and the end of the matter
Ecclesiastes.debate: Who wrote it and when: some credit Solomon, others a later writer using Solomon’s figure, dating it after the exile [[tbd:002:Book of Ecclesiastes]].

Song of Solomon.author: The title can mean the song is by Solomon (970–930 BC) or dedicated to him; authorship cannot be known with certainty [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.date: If by Solomon, the later 900s BC; otherwise later, but completed before 586 BC [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.to: Israel; it may gather love poetry from different periods [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
Song of Solomon.why: A song celebrating the joy and faithfulness of love between a husband and wife, pictured in the language of a garden like Eden [[ks:18]] [[tosn:Song of Solomon 4:1–5:1]]. It reminds a world that has both idolised and despised sex that love within marriage is God’s good gift [[dl:Song of Songs]].
Song of Solomon.story: Married love points beyond itself. Just as Israel was God’s bride, the church is the bride of Christ [[bible:Ephesians 5:31-32]], and the delight of this song is a small picture of knowing him [[ks:18]].
Song of Solomon.genre: Love poetry, perhaps an anthology or dramatic poetry like Job [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].
structure: Beauty and the strength of love
Song of Solomon.debate: How to interpret it: allegory, drama, or a collection of love songs [[tbd:019:Song of Solomon]].

Isaiah.author: Isaiah son of Amoz of Jerusalem, whose ministry ran mainly from 740 to 700 BC [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. The book shows signs of unity: “Holy One of Israel” appears 12 times in chapters 1–39 and 14 times in 40–66 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.date: Chapters 1–39 were mostly written by about 700 BC; 37:38 mentions Sennacherib’s death in 681 BC, so some parts come from Isaiah’s later years [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. Chapters 40–66 address the exiles of about 550 BC [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.to: Judah in the Assyrian period, then the exiles in Babylon whom God promises to bring home [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
Isaiah.why: The Holy One of Israel judges sin but will not abandon his promises. Isaiah announces a coming King from David’s line [[bible:Isaiah 9:6-7]] and a Servant who will suffer for the sins of his people [[bible:Isaiah 53:5]] [[ks:19]]. Isaiah has been called the theologian of the Old Testament; his name for God, the Holy One of Israel, comes from his vision of the LORD on his throne [[dl:Isaiah]] [[bible:Isaiah 6:3]].
Isaiah.story: Isaiah sees a new exodus, God’s Spirit poured out, and a new heaven and new earth [[bible:Isaiah 65:17]] [[ks:19]]. The King and the Servant are one person, and the New Testament proclaims him as Jesus [[ks:19]] [[bible:Acts 8:32-35]]. His salvation reaches to the ends of the earth [[bible:Isaiah 49:6]].
Isaiah.genre: Prophetic poetry of great literary beauty, with a historical section in chapters 36–39 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].
structure: The new heavens and new earth
Isaiah.debate: Whether the book has one author or several: many scholars assign chapters 40–66 to a “second” or “third” Isaiah, mainly because Cyrus (539 BC) is named [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

Jeremiah.author: Jeremiah, the prophet from Anathoth, wrote most of it; his secretary Baruch wrote down his messages and may have edited them [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]]. Chapter 52 is an editorial addition, since Jeremiah’s own words end at 51:64 [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.date: During Jeremiah’s ministry, about 627 to 586 BC; he was later taken to Egypt, around 584 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.to: Judah before and after Jerusalem fell, the captives in Babylon (ch. 29), and the Jews in Egypt [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
Jeremiah.why: A prophet with a broken heart warns Judah for decades to turn back to God before Babylon comes. The judgment falls, but God promises a new covenant, with his law written on their hearts [[bible:Jeremiah 31:31-34]] [[ks:20]].
Jeremiah.story: In the new covenant sins are fully forgiven, and a righteous Branch from David will reign [[bible:Jeremiah 23:5-6]] [[ks:20]]. Jesus spoke of this new covenant at the Last Supper [[bible:Luke 22:20]], and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah’s promise in full [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]]. The New Testament quotes Jeremiah about forty times, and the “weeping prophet” is echoed when Jesus weeps over Jerusalem [[dl:Jeremiah]] [[bible:Luke 19:41-44]].
Jeremiah.genre: Prophetic poetry and sermons, with history of Jeremiah’s sufferings and symbolic acts [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
structure: Symbolic acts and sufferings before the siege
Jeremiah.debate: The order of the messages is not chronological and cannot be fully explained; the Greek Septuagint is about 2,700 words shorter and places chapters 46–51 after 25:13 [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].

Lamentations.author: Traditionally Jeremiah, as the Septuagint and Latin Vulgate say; shared phrases such as “terrors on every side” and “wormwood” support it [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]]. The poems do not name their author [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.date: Shortly after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC; its vivid detail suggests an eyewitness [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.to: The Jews who had lived through the fall of Jerusalem, to give them words for their grief [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.why: Five poems of grief over fallen Jerusalem. They admit that the people sinned, and still they turn to God, because the one who judged them is the only one who can save them [[ks:21]].
Lamentations.story: At its centre is hope: the LORD’s loving kindnesses never fail, and they are new every morning [[bible:Lamentations 3:22-23]]. Its grief finds its answer in Jesus, who bore God’s judgment for his people and rose again [[ks:21]]. The New Testament shows Jesus as the divine warrior who defeated the real enemy of God’s people on the cross [[dl:Lamentations]] [[bible:Colossians 2:15]].
Lamentations.genre: Five poems forming a formal dirge; chapters 1–4 are acrostics on the Hebrew alphabet [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].
Lamentations.debate: Whether Jeremiah wrote it, and why the poems use such complex alphabet patterns (perhaps to aid memory, or to express completeness) [[tbd:012:Lamentations, Book of]].

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel son of Buzi, of a priestly family, taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin when he was about 25 [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.date: His first vision came in 593 BC [[tosn:Ezekiel 1:2]]; the latest dated message is from the 27th year of exile, about 571 BC [[bible:Ezekiel 29:17]].
Ezekiel.to: The exiles settled at Tel-abib by the Kebar canal, who hoped for a quick return home [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.why: A priest in exile sees God’s glory leave the temple because of the people’s sin [[bible:Ezekiel 10:18]], and later sees it return [[bible:Ezekiel 43:4-5]]. God promises a new heart and his own Spirit within his people [[bible:Ezekiel 36:26-27]] [[ks:22]].
Ezekiel.story: Dry bones come to life [[bible:Ezekiel 37:5]], a good shepherd from David’s line will care for God’s flock [[bible:Ezekiel 34:23]], and God will live among his people [[ks:22]]. Revelation takes up Ezekiel’s river of life and holy city [[ks:22]] [[bible:Revelation 22:1-2]]. The New Testament draws on Ezekiel more than sixty times, most of them in Revelation [[dl:Ezekiel]].
Ezekiel.genre: Visions, symbolic acts, parables and oracles, arranged by subject and by date [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]].
Ezekiel.debate: How chapters 34–48 are fulfilled beyond the return from exile: for Israel in the future, or in God’s work among all who share Abraham’s faith [[tbd:005:Ezekiel, Book of]]. The identity of Gog is also debated [[tosn:Ezekiel 38:1–39.29]].

Daniel.author: The book does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition held that Daniel wrote it all, and chapters 7–12 speak in his voice [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.date: The stories run from about 605 BC to the early years of Cyrus, who took Babylon in 539 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]]. The conservative view dates the book to the 500s BC; another view dates it to about 165 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.to: Jews living in exile under foreign rule, and later those suffering under Antiochus Epiphanes (175–163 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.why: Faithful in a foreign land. Daniel and his friends refuse to bow to other gods, and God shows that he rules over every king and empire [[bible:Daniel 4:34-35]] [[ks:23]]. One message rings through every chapter: whatever the circumstances, God is sovereign and will overcome evil [[dl:Daniel]].
Daniel.story: Daniel sees one like a son of man receive an everlasting kingdom [[bible:Daniel 7:13-14]], the title Jesus used most for himself [[ks:23]] [[bible:Mark 14:62]]. It also gives one of the clearest promises of resurrection in the Old Testament [[bible:Daniel 12:2]].
Daniel.genre: Stories and visions; in the Hebrew Bible it sits among the Writings, not the Prophets. Daniel 2:4–7:28 is in Aramaic [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]].
Daniel.debate: Its date (500s BC or about 165 BC), the identity of Darius the Mede, the four kingdoms, and the seventy sevens [[tbd:002:Book of Daniel]] [[tosn:Daniel 9:24–27]].

Hosea.author: Hosea, whose ministry lasted at least 38 years, about 753 to 715 BC [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.date: The late eighth century BC [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.to: The northern kingdom of Israel in its last years; Hosea is the only writing prophet who lived and preached there [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
Hosea.why: God tells Hosea to love an unfaithful wife, a living picture of how God keeps loving Israel when it runs to other gods [[bible:Hosea 3:1]] [[ks:24]].
Hosea.story: After judgment comes restoration: Israel will return to the LORD and to David their king [[bible:Hosea 3:5]] [[ks:24]]. Matthew sees “out of Egypt I called my son” fulfilled in Jesus [[tosn:Hosea 11:1]] [[bible:Matthew 2:15]]. Paul and Peter use the names of Hosea’s children to show that people who were not God’s people are now welcomed in [[dl:Hosea]] [[bible:1 Peter 2:10]], and Paul borrows Hosea’s taunt to death to celebrate the resurrection [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:55]].
Hosea.genre: Hosea’s marriage as a living sign, followed by prophecies mostly in the order given [[tosn:Hosea 4:1–14.9]] [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].
structure: Love that will not let go
Hosea.debate: How to understand Hosea’s marriage to Gomer, and whether the passages about Judah and future blessing are original; most scholars accept the book’s unity [[tbd:008:Hosea, Book of]].

Joel.author: Joel son of Pethuel; Scripture tells us nothing more about either, and the name was common [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.date: Uncertain: some date it after Nehemiah rebuilt the walls (around 400 BC), others earlier [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.to: Judah and Jerusalem after a locust plague worse than any before [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]].
Joel.why: A locust plague becomes a warning of the coming day of the LORD and a call to return to God with all your heart, for he is gracious and merciful [[bible:Joel 2:12-13]] [[ks:24]].
Joel.story: God promises to pour out his Spirit on all people [[bible:Joel 2:28]], and Peter says this came true at Pentecost [[bible:Acts 2:16-21]] [[ks:24]]. It answers Moses’ old wish that all God’s people would be prophets with his Spirit on them [[bible:Numbers 11:29]] [[dl:Joel]].
Joel.genre: Prophetic poetry using the language of the day of the Lord [[bsn:Joel 2:28–3:21]].
structure: The locusts and a call to return
The Spirit and the day of Yahweh
Joel.debate: Its date, and whether the invaders of chapter 2 are locusts, a human army or future battles [[tbd:002:Book of Joel]] [[tosn:Joel 2:1–11]].

Amos.author: Amos, a herdsman and grower of fig trees from Tekoa, south of Jerusalem; there is no strong reason to think someone else wrote the book [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.date: Under Uzziah and Jeroboam II (792–740 BC), probably no later than about 760 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.to: The prosperous northern kingdom of Israel; he preached mainly at Bethel [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
Amos.why: A farmer called by God confronts a rich and comfortable nation: worship means nothing without justice and care for the poor [[bible:Amos 5:24]] [[ks:24]]. Its concern for the poor runs on into the New Testament, where James warns the church never to favour the rich [[dl:Amos]] [[bible:James 2:1-5]].
Amos.story: Judgment is coming, but Amos ends with hope: God will raise up David’s fallen tent [[bible:Amos 9:11]] [[ks:24]], which James sees fulfilled as the nations come to God through Jesus [[bible:Acts 15:15-17]].
Amos.genre: Spoken oracles, five visions and a short story from Amos’s life (7:10–14) [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].
structure: Judgement on the nations and Israel
Amos.debate: Whether the visions and oracles were joined later, and whether some passages were added; the evidence does not require it [[tbd:002:Book of Amos]].

Obadiah.author: Obadiah; we know almost nothing about him, not even his father’s name or home town [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.date: Probably just before or around the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.to: Judah, with a message about Edom [[tbd:002:Book of Obadiah]].
Obadiah.why: The shortest book of the Old Testament. Edom stood by and cheered when Jerusalem fell, and God says that pride will be brought low [[bible:Obadiah 1:3-4]] [[ks:24]].
Obadiah.story: It ends with the promise that the kingdom will be the LORD’s [[bible:Obadiah 1:21]] [[ks:24]]. The old rivalry between Jacob and Esau surfaces again when Herod, a descendant of Edom, tries to kill the child Jesus [[dl:Obadiah]] [[bible:Matthew 2:16]].
Obadiah.debate: Its exact date, and its shared wording with Jeremiah 49:7–22 [[tosn:Obadiah 1:2–4]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 49:7–22]].

Jonah.author: Traditionally Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet under Jeroboam II [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]] [[bible:2 Kings 14:25]].
Jonah.date: If by Jonah, during Jeroboam II’s reign (793–753 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.to: God’s people, who needed to learn that his mercy reaches even their enemies [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]].
Jonah.why: A prophet runs from God because he knows God is merciful [[bible:Jonah 4:2]]. God shows that his compassion reaches even Israel’s enemies in Nineveh [[ks:24]]. Pagan sailors and the people of Nineveh respond to God more readily than his own prophet does [[dl:Jonah]] [[bible:Jonah 3:5]].
Jonah.story: Jesus pointed to Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign of his own death and resurrection [[bible:Matthew 12:40]] [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]]. God’s kingdom is not only about judging the wicked but about mercy for the nations [[ks:24]].
Jonah.genre: A story rather than a collection of prophecies, with a psalm-like prayer in chapter 2 [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]] [[tosn:Jonah 2:1–9]].
Jonah.debate: Whether it is history or a parable, and whether a later author wrote it; many scholars have defended its historical accuracy, and Jesus spoke of Jonah and Nineveh as real [[tbd:002:Book of Jonah]] [[bible:Matthew 12:41]].

Micah.author: Micah of Moresheth, a frontier town near Gath; he is named only in Micah 1:1 and Jeremiah 26:18 [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.date: Under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (about 750–686 BC), though probably not that whole time; some messages come before Samaria fell in 722 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.to: Everyone, but especially Jerusalem and Samaria, land-grabbers, false prophets, judges, priests and dishonest merchants [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.why: Micah warns of judgment on injustice and empty worship, and sums up what God asks: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with your God [[bible:Micah 6:8]] [[ks:24]].
Micah.story: He names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a ruler whose origins are from of old [[bible:Micah 5:2]], quoted when Jesus was born [[tosn:Micah 5:2]]. It ends in praise of a God who delights in mercy and throws sins into the depths of the sea [[bible:Micah 7:18-19]]. Micah also sees the nations streaming to God’s mountain in the last days, beating their swords into ploughshares [[bible:Micah 4:1-3]] [[dl:Micah]].
Micah.genre: About 20 separate messages of judgement and hope [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].
Micah.debate: Its many sections may come from different times, so it is hard to state a single message [[tbd:002:Book of Micah]].

Nahum.author: Nahum the Elkoshite; Elkosh is probably an unknown town, perhaps Elcesi in Judah [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.date: Probably the mid-600s BC, after Thebes fell (about 663 BC) and while Assyria still dominated Judah [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.to: Judah under Assyrian domination [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.why: The fall of cruel Nineveh, which had returned to its violence after Jonah’s day. God is slow to anger but will not let evil go on forever, and he is a stronghold for those who trust him [[bible:Nahum 1:3]] [[bible:Nahum 1:7]] [[ks:24]].
Nahum.story: Nineveh fell in 612 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]]. Nahum shows the King who protects his people and brings down oppressors, a hope fulfilled at last when every evil power is overthrown [[ks:24]]. In the New Testament the warrior God fights a different enemy: Christ defeats the spiritual powers of evil [[dl:Nahum]] [[bible:Ephesians 6:12]].
Nahum.genre: A long poem about the fall of a city [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].
Nahum.debate: Its date: some place it close to 612 BC, and scholars who doubt prophecy date it after Nineveh’s fall [[tbd:002:Book of Nahum]].

Habakkuk.author: Habakkuk the prophet; we know very little about him beyond this book, and the musical notes in chapter 3 suggest he may have been a Levite [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.date: Probably begun between 612 and 605 BC and continued under King Jehoiakim (609–598 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.to: Judah in one of the hardest periods of its history, after Josiah’s death [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.why: A prophet asks God hard questions about evil, and God answers. Habakkuk learns to wait in faith: the righteous will live by faith [[bible:Habakkuk 2:4]] [[ks:24]].
Habakkuk.story: He ends by choosing joy in God even if everything fails [[bible:Habakkuk 3:17-18]]. Paul builds on Habakkuk’s words in his teaching on faith [[bible:Romans 1:17]] [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]]. At the cross people mocked, asking where God was; Jesus trusted him, and God answered by raising him from the dead [[dl:Habakkuk]] [[bible:Matthew 27:43]].
Habakkuk.genre: A dialogue with God, five woes and a closing psalm-prayer [[tbd:002:Book of Habakkuk]].
Habakkuk.debate: Its exact date, and whether 2:4 means faith or faithfulness; the Hebrew ’emunah carries both steadfastness and trust [[tosn:Habakkuk 2:4]].

Zephaniah.author: Zephaniah, whose name means “he whom the Lord protects or hides”; his family line is unusually long, and some think his great-great-grandfather was King Hezekiah [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.date: Under King Josiah (640–609 BC), likely around 630 BC, before Nineveh fell in 612 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.to: Judah, still marked by the idolatry of Manasseh’s reign [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.why: The day of the LORD is near, and it will sweep away pride and idolatry. Yet a humble remnant will find shelter in him [[bible:Zephaniah 2:3]] [[ks:24]].
Zephaniah.story: It ends with one of the most tender pictures in the Bible: the LORD in the midst of his people, rejoicing over them with singing [[bible:Zephaniah 3:17]] [[ks:24]]. Its day of the LORD becomes in the New Testament the day of Christ, when he returns to set all things right [[dl:Zephaniah]] [[bible:Philippians 1:6]].
Zephaniah.genre: Prophetic poetry centred on the day of the Lord [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].
Zephaniah.debate: Whether Scythian invasions, described by Herodotus, lie behind the book; there is no solid evidence [[tbd:002:Book of Zephaniah]].

Haggai.author: Haggai, one of the Jewish settlers in Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1–2; 6:14); he repeatedly states that God spoke to him [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.to: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest and the people who had returned from exile [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.why: Back from exile, the people are building their own houses while God’s house lies in ruins [[bible:Haggai 1:4]]. Haggai calls them to put God first and promises that God is with them [[bible:Haggai 1:13]] [[ks:24]]. God promises that the glory of the new temple will be greater than the old, even though it looked so much poorer [[dl:Haggai]] [[bible:Haggai 2:3-9]].
Haggai.story: God promises to shake the nations and fill this house with glory [[bible:Haggai 2:7]] [[ks:24]], a glory that may point to the Messiah who came to the temple [[tosn:Haggai 2:9]].
Haggai.genre: Four dated prophetic messages [[tbd:008:Haggai, Book of]].
Haggai.debate: What the promise to Zerubbabel as God’s signet ring meant, since he soon disappears from the biblical record [[tosn:Haggai 2:21]].

Zechariah.author: Zechariah son of Berechiah; his name likely means “the Lord remembers” [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]]. Chapters 9–14 do not name him, and most scholars place them later in his ministry [[tosn:Zechariah 9:1–14.21]].
Zechariah.date: Chapters 1–8 date from 520 to 518 BC; chapters 9–14 carry no dates [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.to: The returned exiles, who had not yet rebuilt the temple [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.why: Visions to encourage a discouraged people: rebuild the temple, return to God, and know that his kingdom will come [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]] [[ks:24]]. Its king comes humbly, is pierced and struck as a shepherd, and yet will reign over all the earth [[dl:Zechariah]].
Zechariah.story: Zechariah sees a humble king coming on a donkey [[bible:Zechariah 9:9]], one who is pierced [[bible:Zechariah 12:10]], and the day the LORD will be King over all the earth [[bible:Zechariah 14:9]] [[ks:24]]. The Gospels quote these chapters in telling of Jesus’ suffering [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.genre: Visions explained by an angel, oracles, and in chapters 9–12 apocalyptic writing [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].
Zechariah.debate: When chapters 9–14 were written, and how to interpret the shepherd passages; dating them is only a guess [[tbd:026:Zechariah, Book of]].

Malachi.author: Malachi, a name meaning “my messenger”; since the word appears in 3:1, some think it is a title rather than a name [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.date: Probably just after 433 BC, when Nehemiah returned to Persia; Malachi addresses the same sins as Nehemiah 13 [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.to: The people and priests of Judah after the return from exile, who doubted God’s love and justice [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].
Malachi.why: God’s last word in the Old Testament: I have loved you [[bible:Malachi 1:2]]. He calls a tired people back to honest worship and promises a messenger who will prepare the way for the Lord [[bible:Malachi 3:1]] [[ks:24]].
Malachi.story: Malachi looks to the day when God’s name will be great among the nations [[bible:Malachi 1:11]] and promises Elijah before the great day [[bible:Malachi 4:5]] [[ks:24]]. The New Testament opens with John the Baptist fulfilling that promise [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]]. Mark’s Gospel opens with Malachi’s promised messenger, and Jesus himself names John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come [[dl:Malachi]] [[bible:Mark 1:2]] [[bible:Matthew 11:14]].
Malachi.genre: Sermons in the form of disputations: God states a truth, the people object, God answers [[tosn:Malachi 1:2–5]].
Malachi.debate: Whether Malachi is a personal name or a title; an ancient tradition identified the messenger with Ezra [[tbd:013:Malachi, Book of]].

Matthew.author: The Gospel does not name its author, but the ancient church held it was the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, the tax collector (Matthew 9:9) [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]]. Only this Gospel calls Matthew a tax collector, and it shows a writer who knew about coins and taxes [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.date: Most scholars place it before Jerusalem fell in AD 70, since 24:15 speaks of the temple as still standing. Irenaeus said Matthew wrote while Peter and Paul were in Rome, which would mean the 60s [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.to: Greek-speaking Jewish Christians, perhaps in Antioch in Syria, surrounded by neighbours hostile to the claims about Jesus. Matthew shows that Jesus is the Messiah Israel was waiting for [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.why: The Gospel of fulfilment. Jesus is the long-promised King, the son of David and son of Abraham [[bible:Matthew 1:1]], and in him the kingdom of heaven has come near [[bible:Matthew 4:17]] [[ks:25]]. Together with Mark, Luke and John it gives the foundational witness to Jesus’ life, teaching, death and resurrection [[cm:Matthew]].
Matthew.story: It bridges the two Testaments, showing again and again that Jesus fulfils what the prophets promised [[ks:25]]. It ends with the risen King sending his followers to make disciples of all nations [[bible:Matthew 28:18-20]], the blessing promised to Abraham reaching the whole world [[ks:25]].
Matthew.genre: A Gospel: the story of Jesus’ life, teaching, death and resurrection, with his teaching gathered into five great sections, such as the Sermon on the Mount (5–7) [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].
Matthew.debate: Whether Matthew or Mark was written first, and so which one drew on the other [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]]; this is part of the wider question of why Matthew, Mark and Luke are so alike in some places and different in others [[tbd:019:Synoptic Gospels]].

Mark.author: John Mark (Acts 12:12), a disciple of Peter. Papias, writing early in the second century, passed on that “Mark became Peter’s interpreter and wrote down accurately… all that he remembered” of the Lord’s words and deeds [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.date: Most scholars date it in the 60s [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]]. An early tradition says Mark wrote in Italy after Peter’s death in the mid-60s, though an earlier date cannot be ruled out [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.to: Probably Christians in Rome. It explains Jewish customs (7:3–4) and speaks to believers suffering persecution, perhaps under Nero from AD 64 [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.why: The good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God [[bible:Mark 1:1]], told at a run. The King has come, with power over sickness, demons and storms, yet he came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many [[bible:Mark 10:45]] [[ks:26]].
Mark.story: In Jesus the kingdom has come, hidden at first like a tiny seed [[bible:Mark 4:30-32]] [[ks:26]]. The turning point is Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ, and the book ends at an empty tomb [[bible:Mark 8:29]] [[bible:Mark 16:6]]. Mark was probably the first to write a Gospel, and by telling the story so plainly as history it ties Christian faith to real events in a real place [[cm:Mark]].
Mark.genre: A Gospel, not meant as a strict chronological biography [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]]. Its climax may be the Roman centurion’s words at the cross: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39) [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]].
Mark.debate: How the Gospel ends: two of the oldest manuscripts stop at 16:8 [[tosn:Mark 16:9-20]], and some think Mark meant to leave readers in awe at the empty tomb [[tbd:013:Mark, Gospel of]]. Also whether Mark was the first Gospel written [[tbd:007:Gospel of Matthew]].

Luke.author: Luke the physician, Paul’s companion (Colossians 4:14). The Gospel does not name him, but the “we” passages in Acts, his second volume, place its writer with Paul, which points to Luke [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]].
Luke.date: Debated. Some date it after AD 70; others before Paul’s death about AD 64, which would explain why Acts ends with Paul still in prison in Rome [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]].
Luke.to: Theophilus, a reader who knew the wider Greco-Roman world better than the geography of Israel; Luke avoids terms a Gentile might find puzzling [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]].
Luke.why: A careful, orderly account of Jesus [[bible:Luke 1:3-4]], the Saviour who came to seek and to save the lost [[bible:Luke 19:10]]. Luke shows God’s kingdom welcoming the poor, outsiders, women and sinners [[ks:27]]. Everything happens because God is working out a plan he set long ago: Jesus “must” preach, suffer, die and rise [[cm:Luke]] [[bible:Luke 24:7]].
Luke.story: Luke is the first half of a two-part work; Acts continues the story [[bible:Acts 1:1-2]]. The risen Jesus shows that all of Scripture, from Moses to the Prophets and Psalms, speaks of him [[bible:Luke 24:44-47]] [[ks:27]].
Luke.genre: A Gospel, opening with a preface on Luke’s careful research among eyewitnesses [[bible:Luke 1:1-4]].
Luke.debate: When it was written [[tbd:012:Luke, Gospel of]], its relationship to Matthew and Mark [[tbd:019:Synoptic Gospels]], and how the census “when Quirinius was governor of Syria” (2:2) fits what is known of Quirinius, who supervised a census of Judea in AD 6 [[tbd:017:Quirinius]].

John.author: The Gospel says it was written by “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:20, 24), and the evidence points most probably to the apostle John [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]]. The writer knew Jewish customs and the places of Jesus’ day well, and his account bears the stamp of an eyewitness [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]].
John.date: Long dated to the last decade of the first century; many now argue for a date before AD 70, since John speaks of the pool of Bethesda as still there (5:2) [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]].
John.to: Believers and seekers alike: “these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” [[bible:John 20:31]].
John.why: Written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name [[bible:John 20:31]]. The Word who was with God and was God became flesh and lived among us [[bible:John 1:1]] [[bible:John 1:14]] [[ks:28]].
John.story: Jesus is the true temple, the bread of life, the light of the world and the good shepherd: everything the Old Testament pointed to finds its fulfilment in him [[ks:28]]. He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world [[bible:John 1:29]]. Telling the same story from another angle, John adds depth to the picture of Jesus the other Gospels give [[cm:John]].
John.genre: A Gospel, with much that is not found in the other three [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]].
structure: The last evening with the disciples
John.debate: When it was written, and how it relates to the other three Gospels; the likeness may come from shared oral tradition rather than from John using them [[tbd:010:John, Gospel of]]. Also the story of the woman caught in adultery, which is missing from the earliest manuscripts [[tosn:John 7:53-8:11]].

Acts.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul, who also wrote the Gospel; the “we” passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16) show the writer travelling with Paul [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].
Acts.date: Debated: many say about AD 85; some date it to the early 60s, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome, since it does not tell of his trial [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].
Acts.to: “Most excellent Theophilus”, a title of respect often used for Roman officials [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]] [[bible:Luke 1:3]].
Acts.why: The risen Jesus pours out his Spirit, and his followers carry the good news from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth [[bible:Acts 1:8]]. The kingdom spreads through the Spirit, prayer and the preaching of Jesus [[ks:27]]. Without it we would know nothing of Pentecost, Stephen, the first church in Jerusalem or how the good news first reached the Gentiles [[cm:Acts]].
Acts.story: Acts links the Gospels and the letters. The blessing promised to Abraham for every family on earth begins to reach the nations [[bible:Acts 3:25-26]] [[ks:27]], and the book ends with Paul in Rome, still proclaiming the kingdom of God [[bible:Acts 28:31]].
Acts.genre: The second volume of Luke’s account, telling how the message about Jesus spread from Jerusalem to Rome (1:8) [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].
structure: Paul’s first journey and the council
Paul’s trials and voyage to Rome
Acts.debate: When it was written, and whether Theophilus was one person or stands for Christians in general [[tbd:002:Book of the Acts of the Apostles]].

Romans.author: Paul, as scholars of every viewpoint agree [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]]. Tertius wrote it down for him (16:22) [[bible:Romans 16:22]].
Romans.date: Shortly before Paul took the collection to Jerusalem, around AD 57–58, while he was in Corinth [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]].
Romans.to: The Christians in Rome (1:7), Jews and Gentiles, a church Paul had not yet visited. Phoebe probably carried the letter [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]].
Romans.why: Paul’s fullest explanation of the good news. All have sinned [[bible:Romans 3:23]], and God makes people right with himself as a free gift through faith in Jesus [[bible:Romans 3:24]] [[ks:29]]. Its one great theme is the gospel, and it is less tied to its own time than almost any other New Testament book, so it speaks very directly to readers today [[cm:Romans]].
Romans.story: God keeps his promise to Abraham, who will inherit the world [[bible:Romans 4:13]] [[ks:29]]. By the Spirit, believers share in a new creation that will one day set all creation free [[bible:Romans 8:19-21]], and nothing can separate them from God’s love [[bible:Romans 8:38-39]]. It also shows how the Old Testament and the New, Israel and the church, belong together in one plan of God [[cm:Romans]] [[bible:Romans 11:25-26]].
Romans.genre: Paul’s most detailed letter, both a careful teaching document and a heartfelt personal letter [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]].
structure: New life in Christ and the Spirit
Romans.debate: What Paul means by “the righteousness of God” and how Jews and Gentiles alike are made right with God through faith [[tbd:012:Letter to the Romans]]; and where the closing praise belongs, after 14:23 or at the end of chapter 16 [[tosn:Romans 16:25-27]].

1 Corinthians.author: Paul, as scholars agree, with Sosthenes [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 1:1]].
1 Corinthians.date: About AD 55, from Ephesus, during Paul’s third missionary journey [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]].
1 Corinthians.to: The church in Corinth, a busy Roman port city and capital of Achaia, divided into groups and influenced by the pagan city around it [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]].
1 Corinthians.why: Paul writes to a gifted but divided church and brings everything back to Christ crucified [[bible:1 Corinthians 2:2]]: their quarrels, their bodies, their worship and their gifts [[ks:29]]. It shows the unchanging gospel being applied to everyday problems in a real church [[cm:1-2 Corinthians]].
1 Corinthians.story: It holds the great chapter on love [[bible:1 Corinthians 13:4-7]] and the earliest written list of witnesses to the risen Jesus [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:3-8]]. Christ’s resurrection is the first fruits of ours [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:20]], and he reigns until every enemy, even death, is defeated [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:25-26]] [[ks:29]].
1 Corinthians.genre: A pastoral letter answering reports from Chloe’s household and the letter the Corinthians had sent Paul with their questions (7:1) [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Corinthians]].
structure: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
1 Corinthians.debate: Head coverings in worship: Paul calls them a long-standing church custom, which most modern interpreters see as based on culture [[tosn:1 Corinthians 11:16]]; and the place of speaking in tongues, which the Corinthians prized too highly [[tosn:1 Corinthians 12:1-14:40]].

2 Corinthians.author: Paul, as is widely accepted [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.date: About AD 56, after Paul left Ephesus and travelled north to Macedonia [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.to: The church in Corinth, after a painful visit and a “letter of tears” that has been lost [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.why: Paul’s most personal letter. God’s power is made perfect in weakness [[bible:2 Corinthians 12:9]], and his treasure is carried in clay jars [[bible:2 Corinthians 4:7]] [[ks:29]]. No letter shows more of Paul the man and the pastor [[cm:1-2 Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.story: Paul serves the new covenant of the Spirit [[bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]. Anyone in Christ is a new creation, and God has given us the ministry of reconciliation [[bible:2 Corinthians 5:17-18]] [[ks:29]].
2 Corinthians.genre: A deeply personal letter: Paul repairs his relationship with the church and restarts the collection for Jerusalem [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]].
2 Corinthians.debate: Whether 2:14–7:4 and chapters 10–13 were once separate letters, and whether 6:14–7:1 belongs where it is [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Corinthians]] [[tosn:2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1]].

Galatians.author: Paul (1:1), once a devoted Jew who had attacked the church [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].
Galatians.date: It depends on where the churches were: an earlier date if Paul wrote to the churches he founded in southern Galatia on his first journey, a later one if to northern Galatia [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].
Galatians.to: The churches of Galatia, in what is now Turkey, troubled by Jewish Christians who taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].
Galatians.why: Paul’s passionate letter about freedom in Christ. We are made right with God by faith in Jesus, not by keeping the law, and Gentiles belong to God’s family by faith [[bible:Galatians 2:16]] [[ks:29]]. Its importance is out of all proportion to its size, because people always drift toward thinking salvation is their own achievement [[cm:Galatians]].
Galatians.story: Christ is the promised offspring of Abraham, so all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s heirs [[bible:Galatians 3:16]] [[bible:Galatians 3:29]] [[ks:29]]. The Spirit produces new life, and its fruit is love, joy and peace [[bible:Galatians 5:22-23]].
Galatians.genre: A sharp, urgent letter that skips Paul’s usual thanksgiving and goes straight to a rebuke [[tosn:Galatians 1:1-5]].
structure: Faith and the promise to Abraham
Galatians.debate: Whether Paul wrote to northern or southern Galatia, which affects its date [[tbd:012:Letter to the Galatians]].

Ephesians.author: Paul names himself (1:1; 3:1), and early Christian writers such as Irenaeus, Polycarp and Ignatius accepted it as his. Some features lead many scholars to doubt this, though they make sense if the letter was meant for several churches [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.date: From prison (3:1; 6:20); most scholars think from Rome, between about AD 59 and 63 [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.to: The Christians in Ephesus and the nearby churches; there are no personal greetings, which fits a letter meant for several congregations [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.why: God’s plan to bring all things together under Christ [[bible:Ephesians 1:9-10]]. We are saved by grace through faith [[bible:Ephesians 2:8]], and Jews and Gentiles become one new people [[ks:29]].
Ephesians.story: The church is God’s new temple, a dwelling for God by the Spirit [[bible:Ephesians 2:21-22]] [[ks:29]]. The letter then shows how that new life looks at home, at work and in spiritual battle [[bible:Ephesians 6:10-11]]. From first to last it is God who plans and gives salvation, and Christ himself is our peace [[cm:Ephesians]] [[bible:Ephesians 2:14]].
Ephesians.genre: A letter whose purpose is praise: it opens like a hymn, “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:3), and grounds its teaching on how to live in its teaching about God [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]].
Ephesians.debate: Whether Paul wrote it, and whether it was meant for Ephesus alone [[tbd:012:Letter to the Ephesians]]; and how the household instructions (5:21–6:9) apply, beginning with the call to all to submit to one another [[tosn:Ephesians 5:22]].

Philippians.author: Paul, with Timothy named at the start, though Timothy probably acted as his secretary [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].
Philippians.date: From prison (1:12–13). Rome around AD 62 is most likely; others suggest Ephesus around AD 55 or Caesarea around AD 58 [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].
Philippians.to: The church in Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia, who had sent Paul a gift by Epaphroditus [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].
Philippians.why: A letter of joy written from prison [[bible:Philippians 1:13]]. At its heart is Christ, who humbled himself to death on a cross and was raised to the highest place [[bible:Philippians 2:6-11]] [[ks:29]]. It is a rare letter to a church Paul is well pleased with, full of thanks for their partnership [[cm:Philippians]] [[bible:Philippians 1:3-5]].
Philippians.story: Every knee will bow and confess that Jesus Christ is Lord [[bible:Philippians 2:10-11]]. Believers already belong to heaven and wait for their Saviour to come [[bible:Philippians 3:20-21]] [[ks:29]].
Philippians.genre: A warm letter of thanks and encouragement, with an early Christian hymn about Christ at its centre (2:6–11) [[tosn:Philippians 2:6-11]].
Philippians.debate: Where Paul was imprisoned when he wrote it: Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea [[tbd:016:Philippians, Letter to the]].

Colossians.author: Paul, with Timothy. The tradition is well established, but many scholars today question it because of its theology and style [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].
Colossians.date: It depends on where Paul was imprisoned: if in Rome, as long held, between AD 60 and 62; more scholars now suggest Ephesus, earlier [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].
Colossians.to: The church in Colossae, which had been taught by Epaphras (1:7) and was threatened by a false teaching [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].
Colossians.why: Christ is supreme. He is the image of the invisible God, and all things were made through him and for him [[bible:Colossians 1:15-16]], so believers need nothing added to him [[ks:29]]. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge [[bible:Colossians 2:3]] [[cm:Colossians]].
Colossians.story: God has rescued us from darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his beloved Son [[bible:Colossians 1:13]]. On the cross Christ triumphed over every hostile power [[bible:Colossians 2:15]] [[ks:29]].
Colossians.genre: A letter answering false teaching by making clear who Christ is, built on the hymn of 1:15–20 [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]] [[tosn:Colossians 1:15-20]].
Colossians.debate: What the false teaching in Colossae was, since Paul never clearly defines it, and who wrote the letter [[tbd:012:Letter to the Colossians]].

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul, with Silas (Silvanus) and Timothy; phrases like “I, Paul” (2:18) show that Paul mainly wrote it. The few scholars who doubt this lack strong evidence [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.date: Probably early in AD 50, from Corinth, about a year after Paul first preached in Thessalonica [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.to: “The assembly of the Thessalonians” (1:1), a young church in Macedonia that Paul had been forced to leave, facing persecution [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.why: Encouragement for a young church facing hardship: keep growing in faith, love and hope [[bible:1 Thessalonians 1:3]] [[ks:29]]. It holds Paul’s fullest teaching on what will happen when Jesus returns [[cm:Thessalonians]].
1 Thessalonians.story: Those who have died in Christ are not lost: when the Lord comes, the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will always be with the Lord [[bible:1 Thessalonians 4:16-17]] [[ks:29]].
1 Thessalonians.genre: A pastoral letter written after Timothy’s good report, praising their faith and answering their questions [[tbd:006:First Letter to the Thessalonians]].
structure: Living to please God and the Lord’s coming
1 Thessalonians.debate: What 4:13–18 teaches about Christ’s return. Paul wrote it to comfort the grieving: all who belong to Jesus will live with him for ever [[bsn:1 Thessalonians 4:13-18]] [[tosn:1 Thessalonians 4:14]].

2 Thessalonians.author: Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy, signed in his own hand (3:17). Some scholars doubt it because it speaks of the future differently from 1 Thessalonians [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.date: Not stated. Most likely soon after 1 Thessalonians, since Silas and Timothy were still with Paul [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.to: “The assembly of the Thessalonians”, still suffering and confused about the day of the Lord [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.why: A follow-up for a church shaken by false rumours: the day of the Lord has not yet come, so stand firm and keep working [[bible:2 Thessalonians 2:1-3]] [[ks:29]].
