Together with 1 Thessalonians it is a main source of the New Testament’s teaching on the last things [[cm:Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.story: When Jesus returns he will put right every wrong and be glorified in his people [[bible:2 Thessalonians 1:7-10]]. Until then the Lord is faithful to strengthen and guard them [[bible:2 Thessalonians 3:3]] [[ks:29]].
2 Thessalonians.genre: A short pastoral letter: stand firm and hold to what you were taught (2:15) [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]].
2 Thessalonians.debate: Authorship and order of the two letters [[tbd:019:Second Letter to the Thessalonians]], and who or what is restraining the man of lawlessness (2:6–7) [[tosn:2 Thessalonians 2:6]].

1 Timothy.author: Paul is named in the first verse, and early church tradition from Irenaeus (about AD 185) links only his name with it; its many personal references to Paul’s life are strong evidence. Some scholars argue against it from its vocabulary, which differs from his other letters [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]].
1 Timothy.date: If Paul wrote it, after his first release from prison in Rome, around AD 61 or 62, and before his second imprisonment [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]].
1 Timothy.to: Timothy, whom Paul had left in charge of the church in Ephesus (1:3) [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]].
1 Timothy.why: Paul guides his young co-worker in caring for a church. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners [[bible:1 Timothy 1:15]], so the church must hold to that truth and live it out [[ks:29]]. Paul writes as a father to a trusted son in the faith [[cm:1 Timothy]] [[bible:1 Timothy 1:2]].
1 Timothy.story: There is one God and one mediator between God and people, Christ Jesus [[bible:1 Timothy 2:5]]. The church is the household of God, the pillar and foundation of the truth [[bible:1 Timothy 3:15]].
1 Timothy.genre: One of the three “Pastoral Letters”, grouped together since the second century: advice on church order, leaders and false teaching [[tbd:016:Pastoral Letters]].
1 Timothy.debate: Who wrote the Pastoral Letters [[tbd:020:Timothy, First Letter to]], and how 2:11–15 on women teaching should be understood [[tosn:1 Timothy 2:12]].

2 Timothy.author: Paul. Even many who doubt he wrote the Pastoral Letters accept that 2 Timothy has genuine parts from him, and the evidence for his authorship is stronger than against it [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.date: Between AD 64 and 67, from prison in Rome, shortly before Paul was martyred under Nero [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.to: Timothy in Ephesus [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.why: Paul’s last letter, written as he faces death. Guard the good news, endure hardship, and preach the word [[bible:2 Timothy 4:2]] [[ks:29]]. Written in the shadow of execution, it shows how a Christian can face death calmly and faithfully [[cm:2 Timothy]].
2 Timothy.story: Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching [[bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]. Paul has fought the good fight and looks to the crown the Lord will give to all who love his appearing [[bible:2 Timothy 4:7-8]] [[ks:29]].
2 Timothy.genre: A kind of last will and testament from the apostle [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].
2 Timothy.debate: Authorship, as with the other Pastoral Letters [[tbd:020:Timothy, Second Letter to]].

Titus.author: Paul (1:1). Modern scholars question this because of its language and style, but many respected scholars defend it [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].
Titus.date: Hard to date: probably after Paul’s release from his first imprisonment in Rome, when many believe he worked in Crete and Greece [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].
Titus.to: Titus, a Gentile convert and one of Paul’s most trusted co-workers, left in Crete to continue the work (1:5) [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].
Titus.why: Appoint good leaders and teach a way of life that fits the good news, because God’s grace has appeared, bringing salvation [[bible:Titus 2:11-12]] [[ks:29]].
Titus.story: God saved us not by our works but by his mercy, through the new birth the Spirit gives [[bible:Titus 3:5]]. We wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ [[bible:Titus 2:13]]. Set among the rough people of Crete, it shows that the good news is for the most unlikely people and changes how they live [[cm:Titus]] [[bible:Titus 1:12]].
Titus.genre: A Pastoral Letter: advice on church order, leaders and false teaching [[tbd:016:Pastoral Letters]].
Titus.debate: Authorship, with the other Pastoral Letters [[tbd:020:Titus, Letter to]].

Philemon.author: Paul, writing as a prisoner for Christ (1:9) [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.date: From prison, probably in Ephesus or Rome, at the same time as Colossians (compare Colossians 4:7–14) [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.to: Philemon, a church leader in Colossae who had come to faith through Paul, with Apphia, Archippus and the church in his home [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.why: A short, personal letter. Paul asks Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, a runaway slave who has become a Christian, no longer as a slave but as a dear brother [[bible:Philemon 1:16]] [[ks:29]]. Paul could have commanded, but he appeals out of love and leaves the choice to Philemon [[cm:Philemon]] [[bible:Philemon 1:8-9]].
Philemon.story: It shows the good news at work in one household: in Christ, people divided by the world become one family [[bible:Galatians 3:28]] [[ks:29]].
Philemon.genre: A short personal appeal, though addressed to many people, not only Philemon [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]].
Philemon.debate: What exactly Paul asks of Philemon; one view is that he wants Onesimus freed and welcomed as a full member of the family [[tbd:012:Letter to Philemon]] [[bible:Philemon 1:16]].

Hebrews.author: Not stated. Some early writers held that Paul wrote it, but its anonymity and its writer’s learning from eyewitnesses (2:3) argue against this. Barnabas was an early suggestion; Luther first proposed Apollos [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
Hebrews.date: Probably before AD 70, since it says nothing of the temple’s destruction and speaks as if sacrifices were still offered; perhaps AD 67–70 [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
Hebrews.to: Jewish Christians, as its early title “To Hebrews” suggests, who had suffered for their faith and were tempted to turn back [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
Hebrews.why: Jesus is greater than angels, greater than Moses and greater than every priest, and his one sacrifice brings full forgiveness [[bible:Hebrews 10:12-14]]. So hold on to him in faith [[ks:30]].
Hebrews.story: Hebrews shows how the Old Testament’s priests, sacrifices and covenant point to Christ, the priest-king who brings the new covenant [[bible:Hebrews 8:6]] [[ks:30]]. Like Abraham, believers look for the city God has prepared [[bible:Hebrews 11:16]] and receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken [[bible:Hebrews 12:28]]. It also teaches us how to read the Old Testament, as one long story whose people, places and practices point to Christ [[cm:Hebrews]].
Hebrews.genre: “The word of exhortation” (13:22), showing that Christ is far greater than Judaism’s greatest heroes [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]].
structure: The new covenant and one sacrifice
Hebrews.debate: Who wrote it [[tbd:008:Hebrews, Letter to the]], and the warning passages such as 6:4–8, among the most challenging in the New Testament [[tosn:Hebrews 6:4-8]].

James.author: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Most scholars identify him as James the brother of Jesus; James the son of Zebedee was killed in AD 44 [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
James.date: Many scholars believe it was written early, possibly AD 45–49, when many Jewish Christians had not yet fully separated from Judaism [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
James.to: “The twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (1:1): Jewish Christians facing trials [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
James.why: Practical wisdom for followers of Jesus. Real faith shows itself in action [[bible:James 2:17]]: in how we speak, how we treat the poor, and how we trust God in trials [[ks:31]]. Its chief warning is against being double-minded, trying to have the best of this world and the next [[cm:James]] [[bible:James 1:8]].
James.story: James has been called the Proverbs of the New Testament, and it echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount [[ks:31]]. Believers live under King Jesus now and wait patiently for his coming [[bible:James 5:7-8]] [[ks:31]].
James.genre: Practical wisdom for the first generation of Christians, written like an Old Testament prophet and full of proverbs [[tbd:012:Letter of James]].
structure: The tongue and wisdom from above
James.debate: How 2:14–26 fits with Paul on faith; James may be correcting a misunderstanding of Paul’s teaching on justification by faith [[tbd:012:Letter of James]] [[tosn:James 2:24]].

1 Peter.author: The apostle Peter (1:1), a witness of Christ’s sufferings (5:1). Silas (Silvanus) helped him write it (5:12), perhaps as his secretary or translator. Some scholars think its Greek too good for a fisherman and that someone else wrote in his name; others disagree [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.date: Probably AD 64 or 65, from Rome, called “Babylon” in 5:13 [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.to: Believers, many of them Gentiles, scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, in what is now Turkey [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.why: Hope for Christians who suffer as outsiders. God has given them a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection [[bible:1 Peter 1:3]], so they can live well and follow Christ’s example [[ks:32]]. Its great theme is hope: suffering lasts only a little while, then comes glory [[cm:1 Peter]] [[bible:1 Peter 5:10]].
1 Peter.story: The church is God’s chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation [[bible:1 Peter 2:9]], a living temple built on Christ [[ks:32]]. Suffering comes first, then glory, as it did for Jesus [[bible:1 Peter 5:10]] [[ks:32]].
1 Peter.genre: A letter much concerned with suffering, echoing more of Jesus’ words than almost any other New Testament letter [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]].
1 Peter.debate: Authorship [[tbd:016:Peter, First Letter of]], and the meaning of Christ preaching to “the spirits in prison” (3:19) [[tosn:1 Peter 3:19-20]].

2 Peter.author: Simon Peter (1:1). Its style differs from 1 Peter, so a trusted co-worker may have gathered Peter’s final concerns [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.date: Probably in Rome, after AD 60 and before AD 70; Peter was martyred about AD 64 [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.to: Perhaps the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1), endangered by teachers promoting immorality [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.why: Peter’s farewell: grow in the knowledge of Jesus, trust the Scriptures, and do not doubt that the Lord will return [[bible:2 Peter 1:19-21]] [[ks:33]]. It shows how wrong belief, such as denying that Jesus will return, quickly leads to wrong living [[cm:2 Peter]].
2 Peter.story: The Lord is not slow but patient, wanting all to come to repentance [[bible:2 Peter 3:9]]. We look for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells [[bible:2 Peter 3:13]] [[ks:33]].
2 Peter.genre: Peter’s final words, a kind of testament for the church [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].
2 Peter.debate: Who wrote it, and its close relationship to Jude, a shortened form of which appears in chapter 2 [[tbd:016:Peter, Second Letter of]].

1 John.author: Traditionally the apostle John. It shares so much vocabulary, style and thought with the Gospel of John that the two are closely connected, and its opening claims an eyewitness (1:1) [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.date: Probably near the end of the first century [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.to: John’s “children”, churches threatened by false teaching [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.why: A letter so that believers may know they have eternal life [[bible:1 John 5:13]]. Walk in the light, love one another, and believe that Jesus came in the flesh [[ks:28]].
1 John.story: God is love [[bible:1 John 4:8]], and he showed it by sending his Son to atone for our sins [[bible:1 John 4:10]] [[ks:28]]. It helps believers tell real faith from counterfeit, so that they can rest in God’s assurance [[cm:Johannine Epistles]].
1 John.genre: A simple but deep answer to false teaching, setting the true way beside the false [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
1 John.debate: Whether “the elder John” Papias mentions was a different person from the apostle [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]]; and the words added to 5:7–8 in a few late manuscripts [[tosn:1 John 5:7-8]].

2 John.author: “The elder” [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]], traditionally John [[tbd:006:First Letter of John]].
2 John.date: In a setting much like 1 John [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]].
2 John.to: “The chosen lady and her children”, probably a church and its members [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]].
2 John.why: A short note to a church: walk in truth and love, and do not welcome teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh [[bible:2 John 1:6-7]] [[ks:28]].
2 John.story: A companion to 1 John, holding truth and love together [[bible:2 John 1:3]] [[ks:28]].
2 John.genre: A brief letter warning a church not to welcome false teachers [[tbd:019:Second Letter of John]].
2 John.debate: Whether the lady is a woman or a church [[tosn:2 John 1:1]].

3 John.author: “The elder”, writing in a setting like the other letters of John [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.date: In a setting like 1 and 2 John [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.to: Gaius, who stayed loyal to the elder [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.why: A personal letter praising Gaius for welcoming travelling Christian workers, and warning about Diotrephes, a leader who loved to be first [[bible:3 John 1:5-9]] [[ks:28]].
3 John.story: A glimpse of everyday life in an early house church, and of how love for one another shows itself in practice [[bible:3 John 1:11]] [[ks:28]].
3 John.genre: A short personal letter asking Gaius to care for travelling missionaries [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].
3 John.debate: The conflict with Diotrephes, who rejected the elder’s authority [[tbd:020:Third Letter of John]].

Jude.author: “Jude… brother of James” (1:1), understood by many as Jude the brother of Jesus [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].
Jude.date: Not stated; probably between AD 60 and 100 [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].
Jude.to: Churches troubled by false teachers [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].
Jude.why: Contend for the faith once delivered to the saints [[bible:Jude 1:3]], stay in God’s love, and wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus [[bible:Jude 1:21]] [[ks:33]]. It reminds every generation that attractive but false teaching will come, and that the truth is worth guarding [[cm:Jude]].
Jude.story: It ends with one of the Bible’s great blessings, praising God who is able to keep us from stumbling [[bible:Jude 1:24-25]] [[ks:33]].
Jude.genre: A short letter urging believers “to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints” [[bible:Jude 1:3]].
Jude.debate: Its quotations from books outside the Bible, the Assumption of Moses and 1 Enoch (1:14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9), and what kind of false teaching it opposed [[tbd:010:Jude, Letter of]].

Revelation.author: John (1:9). The earliest sources say the apostle John, son of Zebedee; Dionysius of Alexandria first questioned this because of its style [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
Revelation.date: Either shortly after Nero (AD 54–68), or near the end of Domitian’s reign (AD 81–96), as Irenaeus said [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
Revelation.to: Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, now western Turkey; John wrote from Patmos, where he was likely exiled for his faith [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
Revelation.why: Visions that pull back the curtain on history. The Lamb who was slain has won the victory [[bible:Revelation 5:5-6]], evil will be judged, and God will make all things new [[bible:Revelation 21:5]] [[ks:34]]. No book shows God’s sovereignty more vividly, and the conquering rider is always the Lamb who was slain [[cm:Revelation]].
Revelation.story: The last book completes the story that began in Genesis. The ancient serpent is defeated [[bible:Revelation 12:9-11]], the whole renewed creation becomes God’s dwelling, and his people will see his face [[bible:Revelation 22:3-4]] [[ks:34]].
Revelation.genre: Apocalyptic prophecy in the form of a letter: “in spirit and inner purpose, a pastoral”, as H. B. Swete put it [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
structure: The risen Christ and letters to seven churches
The end and the new creation
Revelation.debate: How to read chapters 4–22: as about the future (futurist), the course of history (historicist), events of John’s own time (preterist), or a symbolic message (idealist) [[tbd:002:Book of Revelation]].
